text: What data volume and growth rate is expected? (storage size, records, throughput)

choices.text: Small — <10GB data, slow growth, single-node viable
Medium — 10GB–1TB, moderate growth, needs partitioning
Large — 1TB–100TB, rapid growth, requires distributed architecture
Massive — 100TB+, petabyte-scale, data lifecycle management needed

answer:
Data volume and growth:

Current scale: 67 questions × 3-5 follow-up choices = 201-335 total options. 7 series, 25 rounds. The framework is static and small (~50KB JSON).

Session data: ~10KB per completed session (67 answers × ~100 bytes average text + follow-up selections + metadata). With 10 sessions per project, that's ~100KB per project.

Workspace projection: A developer working on 50 projects over 2 years would accumulate ~5MB of session data. This is trivial by any storage standard.

Growth rate: Linear with usage. No exponential growth patterns. No data compounding across sessions. Each session is independent.

Data lifecycle: Sessions are immutable after completion (no editing). Exports are regenerated on demand. No garbage collection needed — all data is useful and small.

If the system were to scale to team use (multiple users, shared projects), data volume would grow by a factor of N (team size). At 10 users × 50 projects × 10 sessions, that's ~50MB — still trivial. The SQLite adapter would become relevant at this scale for query performance across sessions.

variants.architect: SPACE's data model is compact by design. The `FrameworkDefinition` (67 questions, 7 series, 25 rounds) is static JSON loaded once at initialization via `loadFrameworkFromV1()` in `src/data/framework-loader.ts`. Session state (`SessionState` in `src/types/index.ts`) grows linearly with answers: each `AnswerEntry` stores `question_id`, `series_id`, `round`, `open_ended_text`, `multi_choice_id`, and metadata — roughly 100-200 bytes per answer. A complete session (67 answers) is ~10-15KB of JSON. The `ArtifactDictionary` accumulates derived values from answers — typically 20-50 artifacts at ~500 bytes each, totaling ~25KB. Snapshots (created at round/series boundaries via `snapshot-manager.ts`) duplicate the full session state, creating a copy-on-write pattern. With 5 series × 3 rounds = ~15 snapshots per completed session, plus manual snapshots, storage grows to ~200KB per session. The `StorageProvider` interface (`src/storage/types.ts`) defines no TTL, no compaction, no partitioning — data accumulates linearly. The `FileSystemStorage` organizes data as `{baseDir}/{project_id}/sessions/{session_id}/state.json` with separate snapshot directories, creating a natural partition boundary at the project level. Growth rate is strictly linear: N projects × M sessions × ~200KB. At 100 projects × 10 sessions, total storage is ~200MB — well within single-node capacity indefinitely.
variants.practitioner: Concrete storage accounting: `SessionState` contains `session: SessionMeta` (~200B), `answers: Record<string, AnswerEntry>` (67 entries × 150B = ~10KB), `progress: ProgressState` (~300B), `artifacts: ArtifactDictionary` (~25KB), and optional `llm_metadata` (~100B). Total per session: ~36KB JSON. The `FileSystemStorage` at `src/storage/filesystem.ts` writes this as pretty-printed JSON (`JSON.stringify(session, null, 2)`) with a 2x size multiplier — so ~72KB on disk. Snapshots duplicate the full state: `Snapshot.state` is the complete `SessionState`, adding another ~72KB per snapshot. With `auto_save_interval_ms` at 10000ms (from `src/config/defaults.ts`), a 30-minute session generates ~180 auto-saves, but since snapshots only trigger at round/series completion (`'round_complete' | 'series_complete' | 'manual' | 'auto'` per `types/index.ts`), actual snapshot count is ~15-20 per completed session. The `projects_dir` default is `~/.space/projects/`, and the `SQLiteStorage` adapter (`src/storage/sqlite.ts`) is available but not the default. Growth projection: a team of 5 developers × 50 projects × 3 sessions × 72KB = ~54MB annually. Growth rate: sub-MB/month for typical individual usage. No compaction needed; no archival strategy needed; no partitioning needed.
variants.strategist: The data volume profile makes SPACE essentially free to operate from a storage perspective. The entire framework definition is ~50KB. A completed specification session produces ~200KB of structured data. Exported specifications (JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML) are ~10-50KB each. Total data footprint for a year of active use: under 10MB. This has zero cost implications — no cloud storage, no database licensing, no backup infrastructure. The simplicity of JSON-on-filesystem storage also means zero operational burden: users can back up projects by copying a directory, share sessions via email, and version-control outputs with Git. The `GitIntegration` class (`src/integration/git.ts`) already supports auto-commit with `[space]` prefix. For market positioning, this small footprint enables 'spec-as-code' workflows where specification files live alongside source code in the same repository. The growth rate analysis matters for team adoption: at 50MB/year per developer, an organization of 1000 developers generates 50GB/year of specification data — trivially manageable with existing infrastructure. Success metric: storage should never be a topic of conversation. If users start asking about disk usage, something has gone wrong in the architecture (probably unbounded snapshot creation or accumulated exports). The `SQLiteStorage` adapter exists for future queryability needs but should remain opt-in.
variants.critic: The 'trivially small' data profile masks a real issue: there's no data lifecycle management at all. `FileSystemStorage.deleteSession()` exists but is never called automatically. Snapshots accumulate without bound — the `saveSnapshot()` method in `snapshot-manager.ts` creates a new snapshot file on every trigger with no deduplication and no pruning. If a user completes 5 series × 3 rounds × 2 (round + series snapshots) = 30 snapshots per session, each at 72KB, that's 2.1MB of snapshot data per session. Over 100 sessions, that's 210MB of snapshot-only data — still manageable, but it's 10x the session state itself. The `pretty-printed JSON.stringify` doubles on-disk size compared to minified JSON — an unnecessary overhead for files that are only read by the application, never by humans. The `ProjectArchive` type in `types/index.ts` bundles sessions and exports together, creating potential for data duplication if archives are exported alongside source sessions. The `SQLiteStorage` adapter (`src/storage/sqlite.ts`) provides better query performance for cross-session analytics but isn't the default, creating a fragmented storage story. The `exportToFiles()` function writes to `output_dir` with no cleanup — repeated exports accumulate files. There's no `.gitignore` awareness: exported files in the project directory would pollute repositories. Growth projections assume ideal usage; in practice, users will create abandoned sessions, duplicate projects, and accumulate exports that they never clean up.

text: What availability, uptime, and disaster recovery targets are required?

choices.text: Best-effort — no formal SLA, occasional downtime acceptable
Standard — 99.9% uptime, daily backups, basic DR plan
High — 99.99% uptime, multi-region redundancy, automated failover
Critical — 99.999%+ uptime, active-active, zero-data-loss DR

answer:
Availability and disaster recovery:

Availability target: Best-effort. No formal SLA. The system is a local development tool, not a production service. Occasional downtime (crash, bug) is acceptable and expected.

Data durability: High. Session data is written to disk after each answer (checkpoint). Crash recovery loses at most one answer (the most recent un-saved answer). The auto-save frequency (after every answer) makes data loss negligible.

Backup strategy: Manual file copy. The entire workspace (~5MB) can be backed up with a single "cp -r ~/.space/projects/ /backup/" command. No database dumps, no snapshot procedures.

Disaster recovery: Copy the backup directory to a new machine. The system has no external dependencies (no database to restore, no service to reconnect). The session files are self-contained JSON — they work on any machine with Node.js.

The simplicity of the storage model (JSON files) makes disaster recovery trivial — just copy the project directory.

variants.architect: SPACE's availability model is best-effort by design. As a local tool running on a single developer machine, 'uptime' is equivalent to 'is Node.js running and does the filesystem work.' There's no server to deploy, no load balancer to monitor, no database to keep healthy. The `createSpace()` factory in `src/engine/core.ts` initializes synchronously — if it fails, it throws and the process exits. The `FileSystemStorage` at `src/storage/filesystem.ts` uses synchronous `writeFileSync`/`readFileSync`, which will throw on permission errors or disk-full conditions but won't corrupt data (atomic writes at the OS level for files < 4KB). The `Snapshot` system (`src/engine/snapshot-manager.ts`) provides automatic snapshots at round and series completion boundaries, creating implicit recovery points. If the process crashes mid-session, the latest snapshot preserves progress up to the last completed round. The `SpaceConfig.auto_save_interval_ms` provides an additional safety net — even without explicit snapshots, auto-saves create a rolling backup. For disaster recovery: sessions live in `~/.space/projects/` as plain JSON files. Backup = copy directory. Recovery = restore files. The `exportArchive()` method in `StorageProvider` creates a self-contained `ProjectArchive` bundle for portable backup. There's no cloud sync, no replication, no automated backup — these are explicitly out of scope for a local tool. The event system (`SpaceEvent` types) provides hooks for external monitoring but ships with no built-in monitoring integration.
variants.practitioner: Reliability mechanisms in the SPACE codebase: (1) The `snapshot-manager.ts` creates snapshots with trigger types `'round_complete' | 'series_complete' | 'manual' | 'auto'` — each snapshot stores the full `SessionState` in a separate file, providing crash recovery up to the last snapshot boundary. (2) `auto_save_interval_ms` (default 10000ms from `src/config/defaults.ts`) triggers periodic persistence via the engine's save mechanism. (3) `FileSystemStorage` uses `writeFileSync` which is synchronous and blocking — for files under 4KB (typical session state), this is effectively atomic on most filesystems (ext4, NTFS, APFS). (4) The `SessionMeta.status` field tracks `'created' | 'in_progress' | 'completed' | 'abandoned'` — sessions interrupted by crash remain `'in_progress'` and can be resumed via `resumeSession()`. (5) The `exportArchive()`/`importArchive()` pair on `StorageProvider` enables full project backup as a single JSON blob. What's missing: no write-ahead log, no fsync guarantees (writes go through page cache), no file locking (concurrent CLI + web access to the same session could corrupt state), no corruption detection (no checksums in `SessionState` or `Snapshot`). The SQLite adapter adds WAL mode and transactional writes but is not the default. Practically, for a single-user tool, the combination of auto-save + snapshots + filesystem atomic writes provides adequate durability. Recovery: find the latest `state.json` or snapshot, load it, and resume.
variants.strategist: SPACE's availability model is deliberately minimal: best-effort, no SLA, no formal DR plan. This is the correct choice for a local developer tool. The 'uptime' equivalent is 'does the tool work when I need it?' — and the answer is yes, as long as Node.js is installed and the filesystem is accessible. The economic argument is compelling: zero infrastructure cost for availability, zero operational overhead, zero on-call burden. The snapshot system provides automatic recovery points without requiring users to understand backup concepts. The `ProjectArchive` format creates a portable, human-readable backup that can be shared, emailed, or committed to version control. For enterprise customers who need more, the `SQLiteStorage` adapter provides transactional durability with WAL mode, and the `GitIntegration` class (`src/integration/git.ts`) enables automatic version control of specification data. The disaster recovery story is 'copy the ~/.space directory' — simple enough that any developer can do it without documentation. Success metric: no user has ever lost work due to a SPACE bug. The auto-save + snapshot combination makes this achievable. For market positioning: 'your data lives on your machine, not in our cloud' is a strong privacy/security selling point for enterprise adoption.
variants.critic: The 'best-effort' label is honest but understates real risks. The `FileSystemStorage` uses `writeFileSync` without explicit `fsync` — data is written to the OS page cache but may not be on disk for up to 30 seconds on Linux (controlled by `dirty_expire_centisecs`). A power loss within this window loses the most recent auto-save. The snapshot system mitigates this: snapshots are written after round/series completion, not on every answer, so a crash between auto-saves loses at most one round of progress. However, `writeFileSync` on a file that already exists is NOT atomic — if the process crashes during the write, the file may be partially written (corrupted). The `readFileSync` in `getSession()` would then fail with a JSON parse error. There's no recovery mechanism for corrupted session files — no backup rotation, no checksum validation, no fallback to the previous snapshot. The `ProjectArchive` export is the only portable backup, but it's opt-in and manual. The snapshot files duplicate the full session state (no incremental snapshots), so a corrupted snapshot doesn't help recover from a corrupted session file — you'd need an earlier snapshot. The `SQLiteStorage` adapter fixes the atomicity issue with WAL mode but isn't the default, creating a reliability gap. The `abandoned` status exists but is never automatically set — interrupted sessions appear as `in_progress` indefinitely, with no automated cleanup or user notification.

text: What scalability model is required? (vertical, horizontal, elastic, serverless)

choices.text: Vertical — scale up a single node as needed
Horizontal — add/remove nodes with load balancer
Elastic — auto-scale based on metrics
Serverless — event-driven scale managed by platform

answer:
Scalability model:

Current model: Vertical. The system runs on a single machine, single process, single thread. Scaling means upgrading the machine (more RAM, faster disk) — but the current requirements are so low that scaling is not needed.

Horizontal scaling: Not needed and not supported. The system is single-user. Multiple users would each run their own instance.

Elastic scaling: Not applicable. The system doesn't have variable load — it processes one session at a time, always.

Serverless: Not applicable. The system requires persistent local storage (filesystem), which doesn't fit the serverless model.

The scalability ceiling is high: JSON files can handle millions of entries before performance degrades. The bottleneck would be the question router's dependency graph traversal, which is O(V+E) where V=7 nodes and E=10 edges — effectively constant time.

variants.architect: SPACE uses vertical scaling exclusively — all state lives in a single Node.js process. The `SpaceInstance` closure in `src/engine/core.ts` holds `sessions: Map<string, SessionState>` in memory, which scales with available RAM. A single session is ~36KB of state; even 10,000 concurrent sessions would consume ~360MB — well within a single process's capacity. The `StorageProvider` interface (`src/storage/types.ts`) is the only abstraction that could support horizontal scaling, but the current `FileSystemStorage` implementation assumes local filesystem access with no distributed coordination. The web server in `web/server.mjs` is a single `createServer` instance with no clustering, no worker processes, no process manager. This is appropriate: the tool serves one user's browser, not a production traffic load. The `LLMProvider` interface in `src/llm/types.ts` is stateless per-request — each `complete()` call is independent, making it trivially parallelizable if needed. The dependency graph traversal and artifact extraction are CPU-bound but operate on fixed-size data (7 nodes, 67 questions) — parallelization would add complexity without benefit. The architecture has no horizontal scaling seams: no session partitioning, no shared-nothing design, no event sourcing. This is a feature, not a limitation — the tool's scope doesn't require it.
variants.practitioner: Concrete scaling analysis: The `createSpace()` function allocates a single `SpaceInstance` with a `Map<string, SessionState>`. Memory per session: `SessionState` ≈ 36KB (answers) + `ArtifactDictionary` ≈ 25KB + snapshot references = ~61KB. Node.js overhead per Map entry: ~100 bytes. At 1000 sessions in memory: ~61MB. The `FileSystemStorage` at `src/storage/filesystem.ts` performs synchronous reads with `readFileSync` and writes with `writeFileSync` — both block the event loop. For the web server path, each HTTP request to `GET /api/session/:id` calls `storage.getSession()`, which reads `state.json` from disk. At 100 requests/sec with 1KB session files, disk I/O is ~100KB/sec — negligible for any modern SSD. The `writeFileSync` calls in `exportToFiles()` (`src/export/index.ts`) are sequential: for N export formats, N sequential writes. The `createProvider()` factory in `src/llm/factory.ts` returns a new provider instance per session, but providers like `OpenAIProvider` are stateless beyond holding an API key. The `execSync` in `GitIntegration.run()` (`src/integration/git.ts`) blocks for up to 10 seconds — this is the only potentially problematic blocking call. Vertical scaling ceiling: the system becomes disk-I/O-bound long before CPU or memory limits. Practical recommendation: don't add clustering, don't add worker threads — the complexity isn't justified.
variants.strategist: Vertical scaling is the right choice for SPACE's market position. The tool runs on a developer's machine — a laptop with 8-16GB RAM and an SSD. The entire system (engine + storage + exports + LLM integration) fits comfortably in <200MB of RAM and <100MB of disk. There's no economic case for horizontal scaling: no cloud infrastructure, no server fleet, no load balancer to maintain. The vertical-only model means SPACE is deployable everywhere Node.js runs: Windows, macOS, Linux, WSL2, Docker containers, CI/CD pipelines. This universality is a competitive advantage over server-bound alternatives. The scalability question is actually a non-question for the current product scope — but answering it well in the generated specification demonstrates understanding. For the specification output, the strategist should emphasize that vertical scaling is a deliberate architectural choice aligned with the product's local-first philosophy. If the product evolves to include team features (shared specs, collaborative editing), the scaling model would shift — but that's a different product. Success metric: SPACE should run smoothly on a 5-year-old MacBook Air with 8GB RAM. If it doesn't, the scaling model has failed. The current architecture achieves this. Don't add Redis, don't add message queues, don't add process managers.
variants.critic: The vertical scaling assumption creates a single point of failure that nobody addresses directly. If the Node.js process crashes, all in-memory sessions are lost (mitigated by snapshots, but snapshots only capture completed rounds, not in-progress answers). The `FileSystemStorage` synchronous I/O model is correct for single-user but creates a hard ceiling: the web server can't handle concurrent requests efficiently because each request blocks on disk reads. The `createServer` callback in `web/server.mjs` is async, but the underlying storage calls are sync — this creates a mismatch where the event loop appears free but is actually blocked during file operations. The `execSync` in `GitIntegration.run()` is particularly concerning: it blocks the entire event loop for up to 10 seconds per git operation. If auto-commit is triggered during a web request, the request will hang. There's no process isolation between the CLI and web server when they share the same `projects_dir` — two processes writing to the same session file will corrupt it. The `SQLiteStorage` adapter adds better concurrency control (WAL mode allows concurrent reads) but still assumes a single process. The real scaling concern isn't throughput — it's the absence of any documentation or enforcement of single-process access constraints. Users might accidentally run both CLI and web server simultaneously against the same data directory.

text: What security and compliance standards must be met? (auth, encryption, audit, regulations)

choices.text: Basic — password auth, TLS, no formal compliance requirements
Standard — OAuth2/MFA, encryption at rest, audit logging
Regulated — SOC2, HIPAA, GDPR, or PCI-DSS requirements
High-security — air-gapped, FIPS, zero-trust architecture

answer:
Security and compliance:

Authentication: None. The system is single-user, local-only. No login, no passwords, no tokens.

Authorization: None needed. Single user has full access to all features.

Encryption: None for local storage. Data is stored as plaintext JSON files on the user's filesystem. This is appropriate for a local development tool — the user's filesystem permissions provide the access control.

Encryption in transit: TLS for LLM API calls (handled by the HTTP client). The system sends user answers to LLM providers over HTTPS. No sensitive data is transmitted beyond what the user explicitly sends.

Input validation: Follow-up selections are validated against the question's choices array. Answer text is stored as-is (no sanitization needed for local storage). Framework JSON is parsed with JSON.parse (throws on malformed input).

No compliance requirements: The system processes no personal data beyond what the user voluntarily enters. No GDPR, HIPAA, SOC2, or PCI-DSS requirements apply. No analytics, no telemetry, no tracking.

Security posture: Minimal attack surface. No network exposure (except optional LLM API calls). No user input processing beyond text storage. No file upload. No database queries. The system is as secure as a text editor.

variants.architect: SPACE's security model is minimal by design, appropriate for a local development tool. The attack surface is small: (1) No network listener by default — the CLI path has no HTTP server. The web server (`web/server.mjs`) binds to localhost only with permissive CORS (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`). (2) No user input processing beyond text storage — answer text is stored as-is in `SessionState.answers[key].open_ended_text` with no sanitization, no HTML escaping, no SQL injection risk (no SQL in the filesystem adapter). (3) No authentication — the `StorageProvider` interface has no auth concepts. The web server has no login, no tokens, no session management. This is correct for localhost-only usage. (4) The `LLMProvider.complete()` method sends user answers to external LLM APIs over HTTPS — this is the only sensitive data transmission. API keys are stored in `SpaceConfig.llm_api_key`, which lives in the application's config but is not encrypted at rest. (5) The `FileSystemStorage` relies on OS filesystem permissions for access control — data files are readable by the running user. There's no encryption at rest, no audit logging, no access control beyond OS-level file permissions. The `Snapshot` type stores full `SessionState` snapshots as plaintext files. For compliance: SPACE processes no PII beyond voluntarily entered text, no financial data, no health data — no GDPR, HIPAA, SOC2, or PCI-DSS obligations apply.
variants.practitioner: Security-relevant code paths: (1) LLM API calls — `OpenAIProvider`, `AnthropicProvider`, `GeminiProvider`, `MistralProvider` in `src/llm/providers/` make HTTPS requests with API keys in headers. Keys are passed via `SpaceConfig.llm_api_key` from `src/config/defaults.ts` defaults or user configuration. No key rotation, no key storage encryption, no key validation beyond checking existence before fallback to `TemplateProvider`. (2) `web/server.mjs` — raw `http.createServer` with manual routing, no helmet, no rate limiting, no input validation middleware. Request bodies parsed via `JSON.parse` with a catch that silently returns `{}` on parse failure — this prevents crashes but could lead to unexpected behavior with malformed input. (3) `GitIntegration.run()` in `src/integration/git.ts` — uses `execSync` with `timeout: 10000` and `stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe']`, preventing stdout/stderr leaking to the terminal but allowing arbitrary git command execution based on `GitConfig`. The `commitMessagePrefix` field is user-controlled and passed directly to git commands — potential for command injection if it contains shell metacharacters (mitigated by `execSync` not using a shell, but still a code smell). (4) `FileSystemStorage` — `writeFileSync`/`readFileSync` with paths derived from `project_id` and `session_id` (both `randomUUID`-based) — no path traversal risk since IDs are generated internally. (5) Export formats (`src/export/formatters/`) — `html-exporter.ts` generates HTML from answer text; if answers contain `<script>` tags, exported HTML is vulnerable to stored XSS if opened in a browser. No HTML sanitization is applied to answer text before export.
variants.strategist: SPACE's security posture is 'secure enough for a local tool' — which is the right level for its market positioning. The tool runs on a developer's machine, processes no sensitive data beyond what the user voluntarily enters, and has no network exposure beyond optional LLM API calls. The security story for enterprise buyers is actually strong: (1) No data leaves the machine unless the user explicitly enables LLM auto-fill. (2) Data lives in plaintext JSON files that can be audited, backed up, and version-controlled. (3) No third-party analytics, no telemetry, no phone-home behavior. (4) The `GitIntegration` class enables automatic version control of specification data, providing audit trails. For adoption strategy, this zero-telemetry, local-first model is a selling point for regulated industries (finance, healthcare, government) where SaaS tools face procurement barriers. The lack of encryption at rest is acceptable because the data (project specifications) is not inherently sensitive — it describes what a system should do, not who uses it. However, if users start storing credentials, API keys, or PII in their specification answers, the lack of encryption becomes a real concern. Success metric: zero security incidents attributable to SPACE's architecture. The current model achieves this by having minimal attack surface.
variants.critic: The security model has several unaddressed risks that become real as the tool matures. (1) Stored XSS via exported HTML: `html-exporter.ts` renders answer text into HTML without sanitization. If a user writes `<script>alert(1)</script>` as an answer and exports to HTML, the resulting file executes arbitrary JavaScript when opened. This is a real vulnerability if exported specs are shared with non-technical stakeholders. (2) API key storage: `SpaceConfig.llm_api_key` is passed in memory and potentially persisted in config files with no encryption. The `createProvider()` factory in `src/llm/factory.ts` creates a new provider instance per session, but the key lives in the config object which persists for the process lifetime. (3) The web server's CORS policy (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`) allows any website to make requests to the local server. If a user has the SPACE web server running and visits a malicious site, that site can read their session data via fetch requests to `localhost:8888`. This is a classic localhost CSRF/exfiltration attack. (4) `GitIntegration` commits specification data with no `.gitignore` awareness — users might accidentally push API keys or sensitive text embedded in their specification answers to public repositories. (5) No audit trail: the `SpaceEvent` system provides hooks but ships with no logging implementation. For a tool used in regulated environments, the absence of access logging and change history (beyond git) is a compliance gap. (6) The `FileSystemStorage` stores data as plaintext — no encryption at rest means any process with filesystem access can read specification data. For a local tool, this is acceptable, but it's worth documenting as a limitation.

text: What external systems, APIs, or services must this system integrate with?

choices.text: No integrations — fully standalone system
1–2 integrations — limited surface area for interoperability
3–7 integrations — multiple external touchpoints
8+ integrations — integration-heavy, requiring an API gateway or ESB

answer:
External systems and integrations:

Required integrations: None. The system is fully standalone.

Optional integrations:
1. LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Mistral, Ollama) — for auto-fill feature. Configured per-project via SpaceConfig. Each provider is behind the LLMProvider interface with a factory pattern for selection.

2. Git — for version control of project files. The GitIntegration class (src/integration/git.ts) provides auto-commit, diff, log, branch, and stash operations. Not required for normal operation.

3. npm registry — for package distribution. The system is published as "space-cli" on npm. Users install via "npm install -g space-cli".

No databases, no message queues, no external APIs (beyond optional LLM). The system is deliberately self-contained.

variants.architect: SPACE's integration architecture follows a hub-and-spoke model with the Engine as the hub. The Engine (`src/engine/core.ts`) exposes a `SpaceInstance` interface that CLI, web server, and any future consumers interact with. External integrations are isolated behind purpose-specific interfaces: (1) `LLMProvider` in `src/llm/types.ts` — a clean abstraction with `complete(params: CompletionParams): Promise<CompletionResult>`. The factory in `src/llm/factory.ts` selects from 7 provider implementations (`openai`, `anthropic`, `gemini`, `mistral`, `ollama`, `local`, `none`), each in its own file under `src/llm/providers/`. Adding a new LLM provider requires implementing the 3-method `LLMProvider` interface and adding a case to the switch in `createProvider()`. (2) `StorageProvider` in `src/storage/types.ts` — a 15-method CRUD interface for projects, sessions, snapshots, exports, and archives. Two implementations: `FileSystemStorage` (default, local JSON files) and `SQLiteStorage` (optional, transactional). The web server (`web/server.mjs`) wraps the engine in REST endpoints but doesn't interact with external systems directly. The `GitIntegration` class (`src/integration/git.ts`) wraps `git` CLI commands via `execSync` — it's not behind an interface, making it harder to mock or replace. The `export/index.ts` module provides 5 renderers (JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML, prompt) that are pure functions: `(session, artifacts, framework, format, name, opts) => ExportResult`. No databases, no message queues, no service meshes. The architecture's strength is interface-based extensibility; its weakness is that integrations are optional and can degrade silently (LLM fallback to TemplateProvider).
variants.practitioner: Concrete integration surface area: (1) LLM providers — 5 HTTP integrations via `src/llm/providers/*.ts`. Each implements `LLMProvider.complete()` which returns `Promise<CompletionResult>`. OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral use their respective REST APIs; Ollama connects to `http://localhost:11434`. The `isAvailable()` method checks if the provider is reachable. (2) Git — `src/integration/git.ts` uses `execSync('git ...', { cwd, timeout: 10000 })` for: `init`, `status`, `commit`, `diff`, `log`, `branch`, `stash`. The `GitIntegration` constructor takes a `repoPath` and optional `GitConfig`. (3) npm registry — package published as `space-cli` per `package.json` `'bin': {'space': 'dist/cli/index.js'}`. (4) Web UI — `web/server.mjs` creates HTTP endpoints (`/api/framework`, `/api/projects`, `/api/session/:id`, etc.) consumed by `web/index.html` via `fetch()`. No WebSocket, no SSE, no streaming. (5) Filesystem — `FileSystemStorage` reads/writes JSON files; `exportToFiles()` writes export outputs to `output_dir`. All integration points use TypeScript interfaces (except Git). The `createProvider()` factory pattern in `src/llm/factory.ts` is the canonical extension point for adding new LLM backends. The `StorageProvider` interface is the extension point for alternative persistence backends. No API gateway, no service discovery, no integration testing framework for external dependencies.
variants.strategist: SPACE's integration model is deliberately minimal — the tool is self-contained with optional external connections. This is a strategic advantage in the developer tooling market: zero mandatory integrations means zero setup friction. The npm-based distribution (`npm install -g space-cli`) is the primary channel, requiring only Node.js >= 18.0.0. text: What development process or methodology best fits this project? How should work be planned and tracked?

choices.text: Sprint-based agile (Scrum) — fixed-length iterations with formal ceremonies
Continuous flow (Kanban) — pull-based with WIP limits, no fixed iterations
Lean/startup — build-measure-learn cycles, just-in-time planning

answer:
Development methodology: Iterative, phase-based development with test-driven increments.

Process: Build one feature at a time, test it thoroughly, then move to the next. No big design upfront — the architecture emerged from implementation. Each phase produced a working, tested increment.

Phase breakdown:
1. Core engine + CLI (2 days) — question routing, answer recording, session management, CLI interface
2. Framework data + tests (1 day) — all 67 questions, 112+ unit tests
3. Web UI (1 day) — Tailwind SPA with REST API backend
4. Storage + LLM + Git (2 days) — StorageProvider, LLM factory, GitIntegration
5. Documentation + packaging (1 day) — README, types, npm config, CI/CD

Total: ~5 working days. Each phase built on the previous one. No phase was blocked by incomplete work from earlier phases — they were designed to be independently deliverable.

No formal project management tool. Development tracked via git commits with descriptive messages. No Kanban board, no sprint planning, no standups. The solo developer is both the planner and the implementer.

variants.architect: SPACE's development process maps to the Iterative-Incremental pattern, where each cycle produces a deployable artifact. The architecture supports this through clean module boundaries: src/engine/core.ts defines the SpaceInstance contract, src/storage/types.ts defines StorageProvider, and src/llm/types.ts defines LLMProvider — each can be developed and tested independently. The dependency graph between these modules flows one direction: engine depends on storage and LLM, but neither depends on the other. This unidirectional dependency structure enables parallel development if the team grows. The framework definition in src/data/framework-loader.ts is treated as a versioned, immutable input, following the Infrastructure as Code pattern — changes to the question taxonomy are releases, not edits. The session state machine (created → in_progress → completed) in src/engine/session-manager.ts enforces valid state transitions, which means development can add new features without breaking existing session flows. From a process perspective, the project benefits from feature branching with the GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts providing automated commit hooks. The lack of a formal CI/CD pipeline is an architectural debt that should be addressed: a GitHub Actions workflow that runs vitest, tsc --noEmit, and npm pack would catch regressions before merge. The current ad-hoc process works for a solo developer but creates fragility — if someone introduces a breaking change to ArtifactDictionary or SessionState, the cascade through 112+ tests is the only safety net.
variants.practitioner: The concrete process is test-driven increments aligned with module boundaries. Each feature follows: (1) Define TypeScript interfaces in src/types/index.ts, (2) Implement the module, (3) Write tests in the corresponding test file. The test suite uses vitest (configured in package.json via 'npm test' → 'vitest run') and covers src/engine/, src/storage/, src/export/, src/llm/, src/intelligence/, and src/template/. Session lifecycle code lives in src/engine/session-manager.ts with functions like createSession(), setAnswer(), completeRound(), completeSeries() — each has direct test coverage. The question routing logic in src/engine/question-router.ts uses getCurrentQuestion() and advanceToNextQuestion() which are pure functions and easy to test. Work tracking is git-commit-based: each meaningful change gets a descriptive commit message. The build pipeline is minimal — 'tsc' for compilation, 'vitest run' for tests, no linting step. For a practitioner adding a new export format, the path is clear: implement src/export/formatters/newformat-exporter.ts following the ExportResult interface (content, filename, mime_type), add a case to the switch in src/export/index.ts, and write tests. For adding a new LLM provider, implement src/llm/providers/newprovider.ts satisfying the LLMProvider interface (name, complete(), isAvailable()), and add a case to createProvider() in src/llm/factory.ts.
variants.strategist: The development process choice directly impacts time-to-market and investor confidence. For a developer tooling product, shipping fast matters more than process maturity. SPACE's ~5-day development cycle for a working MVP demonstrates capital efficiency that appeals to bootstrapped founders and seed-stage investors. The process should evolve: Phase 1 (current) is solo iterative — build the CLI, validate with 5-10 users, iterate. Phase 2 should introduce lightweight Kanban for tracking issues and feature requests once there's a GitHub repo with external contributors. Phase 3 adds sprint cadence (2-week cycles) when the team reaches 3-4 people. The current lack of formal process is actually an advantage at this stage — overhead would slow iteration during the product-market fit search. Key process metric: cycle time from idea to deployed feature. Currently this is measured in git commit timestamps. Target: maintain sub-day cycle time through the MVP phase. Risk: the absence of any process documentation means institutional knowledge lives only in code. As the user base grows beyond 100, a CONTRIBUTING.md and architectural decision records (ADRs) become necessary. The process should formalize when GitHub stars exceed 50 or npm weekly downloads exceed 100.
variants.critic: The 'no formal process' approach is fragile in several ways. First, without CI/CD, the test suite only runs when the developer manually executes 'npm test' — there's nothing preventing a broken commit from reaching npm. The build artifact (dist/) isn't verified on every push. Second, the lack of linting (package.json has 'lint': 'echo no linter configured') means code style drift is undetectable. Third, without branch protection or PR requirements, a single force-push could destroy history. The phase-based development described (Core engine → Framework data → Web UI → Storage+LLM → Docs) isn't actually documented anywhere — it's reconstructed from git log. Future contributors can't understand the rationale behind architectural choices without reading commit messages or asking the original developer. The GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts auto-commits with '[space]' prefix, which is useful but doesn't establish conventional commits, making automated changelog generation impossible. The claim that 'no phase was blocked by incomplete work from earlier phases' is aspirational — in practice, the framework-loader.ts dependency means framework data MUST exist before the engine can run. A formal process would have identified this critical path earlier.

text: What is the expected team size, composition, and structure?

choices.text: Solo or pair — 1–2 people, all roles combined
Small team — 3–6 people with distinct roles (dev, design, PM)
Multiple teams — 7+ people across 2+ squads with coordination overhead

answer:
Team size and composition: Solo developer.

The entire system was built by one person in ~5 working days. All roles are combined: architect, developer, tester, documentation writer, release manager.

Why solo works: (1) The codebase is small (~3500 LOC). (2) The domain is well-understood (the developer IS the target user). (3) The architecture is simple (no distributed systems, no complex state management). (4) The test suite provides safety net for changes.

When to add team members: If the project grows beyond 10,000 LOC, or if multiple features need parallel development, or if the web UI becomes a significant application. Currently, none of these apply.

If the team grows: The recommended first hire would be a frontend developer (the web UI is the most likely area for growth) or a DevOps engineer (CI/CD, npm publishing, release automation). The architecture supports team development through clear module boundaries and comprehensive type definitions.

variants.architect: The architecture implicitly encodes team size assumptions. The monolithic SpaceInstance interface in src/engine/core.ts combines session management, question routing, progress tracking, and event emission into a single object — this is the God Object antipattern that works at ~3500 LOC but becomes unmanageable at 10,000+. If the team grows, the first architectural split should separate the Engine (orchestration) from SessionManager (state) from QuestionRouter (flow control), which already exist as separate modules but are composed inside core.ts. The StorageProvider and LLMProvider interfaces in src/storage/types.ts and src/llm/types.ts are clean dependency injection points that enable parallel development by different team members. However, the ExportResult interface in src/export/index.ts is a simple function signature, not a pluggable class — adding a new export format requires modifying the switch statement, which creates merge conflicts with multiple contributors. The template system in src/template/ and the intelligence layer in src/intelligence/ are loosely coupled to the engine, making them good candidates for ownership by separate team members. The current architecture assumes a single writer to ~/.space/projects — there's no concurrency control in FileSystemStorage. For a team of 3+, this becomes a race condition hazard.
variants.practitioner: The codebase maps to clear ownership zones even for a solo developer. Engine layer (src/engine/): core.ts, session-manager.ts, question-router.ts, dependency-resolver.ts, validator.ts, progress.ts, snapshot-manager.ts — the heart of the system, ~800 LOC. LLM layer (src/llm/): factory.ts, providers/*.ts, artifact-synthesizer.ts, quality-scorer.ts, spec-generator.ts, question-refiner.ts — AI integration, ~600 LOC. Export layer (src/export/): formatters/*.ts — output generation, ~500 LOC. Storage layer (src/storage/): filesystem.ts, sqlite.ts — persistence, ~400 LOC. Intelligence layer (src/intelligence/): analytics.ts, completeness-scorer.ts, contradiction-detector.ts, recommendations.ts, adaptive-router.ts — analysis, ~500 LOC. CLI layer (src/cli/): index.ts, commands/*.ts — user interface, ~400 LOC. Each zone has a clear API contract defined by TypeScript interfaces. For a second developer, the recommended onboarding path is: (1) Read src/types/index.ts to understand data model, (2) Read src/engine/core.ts to understand orchestration, (3) Pick one zone and implement a feature. The 112+ tests serve as executable documentation. For a third developer, the web UI (web/ directory) is a standalone target that can be developed independently of the CLI.
variants.strategist: Team size is a product strategy decision, not just a technical one. Currently, solo development is optimal because: (1) Decision speed is maximum — no meetings, no alignment overhead, (2) The product vision is singular and coherent, (3) Costs are near-zero. The growth trigger should be user traction, not internal readiness. When to add the second person: when there are 50+ active users generating issues, or when the feature backlog exceeds 20 items. The first hire profile matters enormously — a frontend developer for the web UI (currently a single HTML file in web/) would have the highest impact because the CLI is already solid. Alternatively, a developer advocate who uses SPACE daily and can write documentation, create tutorials, and manage the community. What NOT to hire for: backend/storage work — the SQLite and FileSystem implementations in src/storage/ are complete and stable. Don't hire a PM until there are 3+ developers needing coordination. Don't hire DevOps until there's a CI/CD pipeline to maintain. Revenue metrics that justify hiring: $5K MRR for first hire, $15K MRR for second, $30K MRR for third. Until then, the solo developer model with occasional contractor support for specific features (e.g., PDF export) is the most capital-efficient structure.
variants.critic: The 'solo developer works because the codebase is small' argument conflates correlation with causation. The real question is whether solo development produces better or worse software than a small team. In SPACE's case, the lack of code review means type-safety issues like ArtifactValue.value being typed as 'any' in src/types/index.ts went unnoticed. The FileSystemStorage in src/storage/filesystem.ts uses synchronous fs operations (readFileSync, writeFileSync) which block the Node.js event loop — a second developer would likely have flagged this. The SQLiteStorage in src/storage/sqlite.ts writes the entire database to disk on every mutation (this.persist() after every operation) — this is O(n) where n is database size and would cause performance degradation as data grows. A team member with database experience would catch this immediately. The GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts uses execSync with a 10-second timeout — if git operations take longer (large repos), this silently fails and returns empty strings. The 'all roles combined' model means the developer is simultaneously architect, implementer, and tester — but testing your own code has well-documented blind spots. At minimum, a peer review process (even asynchronous, via GitHub PRs) would catch architectural issues before they become technical debt.

text: What code review, testing, and quality assurance practices should be followed?

choices.text: Light — ad-hoc reviews, manual testing, minimal automation
Standard — mandatory reviews, unit + integration tests, CI gates
Rigorous — pair programming, TDD, property-based testing, full automation

answer:
Code review and quality practices:

Testing: Test-driven development for core functionality. Every feature has corresponding tests. The test suite (112+ tests) covers all public APIs. Tests run in <2 seconds.

Quality gates:
- TypeScript strict mode — no implicit any, no null bypass, no type assertions unless necessary
- All tests pass before any commit
- No linting violations (eslint not configured — type checking serves this purpose)
- No console.log in production code (test output only)

Code style:
- Consistent naming: camelCase for variables/functions, PascalCase for types/classes, kebab-case for files
- Functional over imperative where possible
- No nested callbacks — async/await throughout
- Early returns over nested ifs
- Types are explicit (no inference where clarity matters)

No formal code review (solo developer). The test suite serves as automated review — if the tests pass, the code is correct. The type system serves as structural review — if it compiles, the types are consistent.

No pair programming. No mob programming. No PR review process. These would add overhead without benefit for a solo-maintained project of this size.

variants.architect: SPACE's quality architecture has three layers that complement each other: TypeScript's type system provides compile-time guarantees, the vitest test suite provides behavioral verification, and the Engine's event system enables runtime validation. The type system in src/types/index.ts is the first line of defense — SessionState, AnswerEntry, ArtifactDictionary, and ExportResult are all explicitly typed, making structural regressions compile-time errors. The 112+ test suite organized by module (engine, storage, export, llm, intelligence) provides coverage of public APIs. However, the architecture lacks a formal testing pyramid: there are unit tests but no integration tests (e.g., testing Engine → StorageProvider → FileSystemStorage end-to-end) and no E2E tests (e.g., testing the CLI via execSync). The SpaceInstance event system (on(event, handler)) in src/engine/core.ts enables runtime quality checks — handlers can validate session state transitions and emit warnings. This is architecturally equivalent to Aspect-Oriented Programming and could support cross-cutting concerns like audit logging without modifying core logic. A quality architecture improvement would be adding a ValidationMiddleware layer between the Engine and StorageProvider that enforces invariants (e.g., session must be in_progress before answer submission) without coupling validation to business logic.
variants.practitioner: The test suite uses vitest with describe/it blocks organized by module. Tests are colocated with source files (e.g., src/engine/core.test.ts tests src/engine/core.ts). The test pattern follows Arrange-Act-Assert: create a SpaceInstance via createSpace(), perform operations, assert results. Key test categories: (1) Session lifecycle tests in core.test.ts — createSession, startSession, resumeSession, submitAnswer, completeRound, completeSeries. (2) Question routing tests in question-router.test.ts — getCurrentQuestion, advanceToNextQuestion, dependency resolution. (3) Storage tests in filesystem.test.ts and sqlite.test.ts — CRUD operations for projects, sessions, snapshots. (4) Export tests in json-exporter.test.ts, markdown-exporter.test.ts, etc. — format correctness. (5) LLM provider tests using NullProvider and TemplateProvider — provider interface compliance. Running the full suite: 'npm test' → 'vitest run', completes in <2 seconds. To add a new test: create a .test.ts file adjacent to the source, import the function, write test cases. No test configuration needed — vitest auto-discovers *.test.ts files. Type checking: 'npx tsc --noEmit' validates all types without emitting files. No ESLint configured — the package.json has 'lint': 'echo no linter configured'.
variants.strategist: Quality practices must be proportional to the product's maturity and user base. For a CLI tool at <100 users, the current approach (TypeScript strict + 112+ tests + manual QA) is sufficient. The ROI calculation: each test takes ~5 minutes to write, 112 tests = ~9 hours, but they prevent regression bugs that would cost 1-2 hours each to fix in production. At 100+ users, the strategy should evolve: (1) Add CI/CD with GitHub Actions running tests on every PR — cost: $0/month for open source, prevents broken releases. (2) Add ESLint with TypeScript-strict rules — catches patterns that TypeScript alone misses (unused variables, console.log in production code). (3) Add integration tests for the CLI — testing 'space init', 'space run --auto', 'space export' end-to-end. Success metrics for quality: (1) Test coverage percentage (target: 80%+ for core modules), (2) Mean time to detect a regression (target: <1 commit), (3) npm publish rejection rate (target: 0%). The current quality investment is high for a solo project but pays dividends in user trust — developer tools live or die on reliability. Quality is the primary competitive advantage against competitors who ship AI-generated specs without validation.
variants.critic: Several quality gaps exist that undermine the stated practices. First, 'no linting violations' is a false claim — ESLint isn't configured, so there are literally no violations because rules aren't enforced. The package.json confirms: 'lint': 'echo no linter configured'. Second, the test suite tests public APIs but has blind spots: the template system (src/template/), the artifact mapping logic (src/data/artifact-mapping.ts), and the dependency resolver (src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts) may have insufficient coverage — there's no coverage report generated. Third, there are no negative tests for edge cases: what happens when the framework JSON is malformed? What if storage disk is full? What if two sessions write to the same project simultaneously? The SQLiteStorage's this.persist() call after every mutation means a crash mid-write could corrupt the database — there's no WAL mode or transaction support. Fourth, 'No console.log in production code' is unverifiable without ESLint's no-console rule. Fifth, the test suite doesn't test error paths: what does createProvider() return when given an invalid llm_provider value? The switch in src/llm/factory.ts falls through to NullProvider, which silently succeeds — a test should verify this behavior is intentional. The test-to-code ratio suggests adequate coverage, but without coverage metrics, it's impossible to verify.

text: How should the team handle technical debt, refactoring, and code quality?

choices.text: Opportunistic — clean as you go, no formal tracking
Budgeted — allocate X% of each sprint to debt reduction
Formal — tracked backlog with dedicated quality improvement cycles

answer:
Technical debt management:

Approach: Opportportunistic — clean as you go, no formal tracking.

Debt prevention: (1) TypeScript strict mode prevents type debt. (2) Comprehensive tests prevent behavioral debt. (3) Small codebase limits structural debt. (4) Clear naming conventions prevent semantic debt.

Debt detection: Code review of own code (rare but occurs). Refactoring triggered by pain points — when adding a feature requires navigating complex code, that code gets simplified first.

Debt priority: High — anything that affects correctness or security. Medium — anything that affects maintainability. Low — anything that affects style or conventions.

Known debt: (1) No ESLint configuration — relies on TypeScript for linting. (2) No Prettier configuration — relies on manual formatting. (3) Some test files have repetitive setup that could be extracted to helpers. (4) The web UI inline JavaScript could be modularized.

Debt payoff: Each refactoring must produce measurable improvement (fewer lines, clearer names, better test coverage, or simpler logic). Refactoring for its own sake is avoided — the YAGNI principle applies.

variants.architect: SPACE's technical debt profile is shaped by its rapid development cycle (~5 days). The architecture has several intentional debt positions: (1) ArtifactValue.value typed as 'any' in src/types/index.ts trades type safety for flexibility — this should eventually become a discriminated union. (2) FileSystemStorage uses synchronous fs operations (readFileSync, writeFileSync) instead of async — acceptable for a CLI tool but blocks if ported to a web server. (3) SQLiteStorage persists the entire database to disk after every mutation via this.persist() — this is O(n) per write and should be replaced with WAL mode or explicit transaction batching. (4) The ExportResult interface lacks a size_bytes field, making it impossible for callers to assess output size without calling .length on the content string. (5) The switch statement in src/export/index.ts and src/llm/factory.ts uses manual dispatch instead of a registry pattern — adding new exporters/providers requires modifying existing code. The engine's event system in src/engine/core.ts uses a simple Map<string, EventHandler[]> — a typed EventEmitter or a middleware pattern would provide better type safety and composability. The dependency graph implementation in src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts is implicit in the framework JSON rather than validated at the type level.
variants.practitioner: Concrete debt items visible in the codebase: (1) src/storage/filesystem.ts:14 — mkdirSync called in constructor, should check existence first (it does via existsSync, but the pattern is inconsistent with sqlite.ts). (2) src/integration/git.ts:27 — execSync timeout is hardcoded at 10000ms, should be configurable via GitConfig. (3) src/llm/factory.ts:7-31 — the switch statement should be replaced with a Map<string, () => LLMProvider> for extensibility. (4) src/export/index.ts:19-30 — same switch pattern, same fix. (5) src/engine/core.ts — the createSpace function is ~150 lines and growing; it should be decomposed into smaller factory functions. (6) src/types/index.ts — ArtifactValue.value typed as 'any'; should be ArtifactValue<string | number | boolean | string[] | Record<string, unknown>>. Refactoring approach: use the Boy Scout Rule — leave code cleaner than you found it. Each time you touch a module, fix one debt item. No dedicated refactoring sprints needed at this scale. The test suite (112+ tests) provides safety for refactoring. Run 'npm test' after each change. For structural refactoring (e.g., replacing switch with registry), create a branch, refactor, run tests, merge.
variants.strategist: Technical debt should be managed like financial debt — track it, prioritize it, pay it down strategically. Current debt inventory: (1) Type safety debt (ArtifactValue.value as 'any') — low priority, causes no user-facing issues. (2) Performance debt (SQLiteStorage persist pattern) — medium priority, will matter when datasets grow beyond 10MB. (3) Extensibility debt (switch-based dispatch) — medium priority, blocks community contributions for new providers/exporters. (4) Testing debt (no coverage metrics) — low priority, tests exist but coverage is unknown. Priority ranking by business impact: (1) Extensibility debt should be paid down before open-sourcing — contributors need a clear pattern to follow. (2) Performance debt should be paid down before 500+ sessions — SQLite write latency will become noticeable. (3) Type safety debt is lowest priority — it's a developer experience issue, not a user issue. Debt budget: allocate 20% of development time to debt reduction once the team reaches 2+ people. For a solo developer, debt is paid down opportunistically. Key metric: track debt items in a GitHub issue labeled 'tech-debt', review monthly, close when fixed. Target: no more than 10 open debt items at any time.
variants.critic: The 'opportunistic — clean as you go' approach has failed to address several significant issues. The codebase has grown organically without a single refactoring pass, and the debt is accumulating: (1) The Engine class in src/engine/core.ts is a monolith that handles session lifecycle, question routing, progress tracking, event emission, and serialization — this violates Single Responsibility Principle and makes the module hard to test in isolation. (2) The StorageProvider implementations (FileSystemStorage, SQLiteStorage) duplicate the ensureDir() utility function — this is DRY violation that suggests the code was copied between files. (3) The GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts uses execSync everywhere, making it impossible to use in an async context — if the web server ever needs git operations, this class must be rewritten. (4) The export system has no validation — exportSession() in src/export/index.ts trusts that the SessionState is complete and valid, which means exporting an incomplete session produces a corrupted spec without warning. (5) There's no migration path for framework version upgrades — if the framework JSON schema changes, existing sessions become unreadable. The 'debt prevention' strategy (TypeScript strict mode, comprehensive tests) is necessary but insufficient. Without static analysis (ESLint, complexity checks, dependency analysis), structural debt accumulates invisibly. The honest assessment: the codebase is in decent shape for its age, but the lack of any formal debt tracking means issues are only discovered when they cause pain.

text: How should the team communicate, share knowledge, and manage decisions?

choices.text: Async-first — written docs, Slack/Teams, minimal meetings
Balanced — regular standups, weekly syncs, supplemented by async
Sync-heavy — daily standups, frequent pairing, co-located or synchronous remote

answer:
Communication and knowledge management:

Solo developer: All communication is with self (current and future). The primary communication channel is code comments and documentation.

Documentation as communication:
- README.md: How to install and use the system
- Type definitions: How the system's data model works
- Test files: How the system's behavior is verified
- Framework JSON: How the question taxonomy is structured

No meetings, no Slack, no formal communication channels. The documentation IS the communication — it's written for the future developer (who might be the same person in 6 months).

Knowledge capture: Every design decision is recorded in code (through naming and structure) or in comments (through "why" explanations). The framework JSON is the canonical source for the question taxonomy — understanding it is equivalent to understanding the system's purpose.

variants.architect: Knowledge management in SPACE is distributed across four artifacts: (1) The framework JSON files encode domain knowledge as structured data — the 326 probes, dependency graph, and artifact definitions in the FrameworkDefinition schema are the authoritative source of project taxonomy. (2) TypeScript type definitions in src/types/index.ts serve as machine-readable architecture documentation — SessionState, AnswerEntry, ArtifactDictionary define the system's contracts. (3) The README.md provides user-facing documentation for installation and usage. (4) Code comments are minimal, consistent with the 'code is documentation' philosophy. The architectural concern is that decisions aren't captured anywhere — why was FileSystemStorage chosen over direct file writes? Why does the Engine emit events instead of using callbacks? Why is the framework stored as JSON instead of TypeScript constants? These decisions are embedded in code but not articulated in ADRs (Architecture Decision Records). For a growing project, this creates knowledge fragmentation: new contributors must reverse-engineer rationale from implementation. The event system in src/engine/core.ts (on/emit pattern) is itself an architectural decision that should be documented — it enables the intelligence layer (src/intelligence/) to observe without coupling, but the trade-off is implicit dependency on event names being stable.
variants.practitioner: Knowledge sharing for a practitioner happens through three channels: (1) README.md — installation ('npm install -g space-cli'), usage ('space init <name>', 'space run <name>'), and architecture overview. (2) Type definitions — src/types/index.ts is the data model reference. Every interface is exported and self-documenting through field names and types. (3) Test files — src/**/*.test.ts demonstrate expected behavior through examples. The test files are the most reliable documentation because they're always in sync with the code. For contributing, the process is: fork the repo, create a branch, implement changes, run 'npm test' and 'npx tsc --noEmit', submit a PR. There's no CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, or issue templates — these are gaps. The CLI commands are documented in src/cli/index.ts via Commander's .description() methods. For the web UI, there's no separate documentation — it's a self-contained HTML file served by web/server.mjs. Knowledge about the framework structure lives in prompt-framework/ as JSON files — the framework-loader.ts parses these. A practitioner extending the framework needs to understand the FrameworkDefinition type and the dependency graph schema.
variants.strategist: Communication strategy should differentiate between internal (developer) and external (user) channels. Internal: For a solo developer, the primary communication artifact is git commit messages — descriptive commits serve as a changelog and decision log. For a team, this needs to evolve to: (1) GitHub Issues for feature requests and bug reports, (2) GitHub Discussions for architectural decisions and questions, (3) ADRs for significant design choices. External: The README.md is the single source of truth for users. It should include: installation, quickstart, configuration, troubleshooting, and contribution guidelines. For community growth, add: (1) A Discord/Slack channel for real-time support, (2) A blog (on dev.to or GitHub Pages) for release announcements, (3) Issue templates for bug reports and feature requests. Knowledge sharing through the framework itself is the most scalable approach — the 326 probes in JSON are inherently shareable and remixable. If another team wants to create their own specification framework, they can author new JSON files without modifying SPACE's code. This is a platform play — SPACE becomes the runtime, and the framework becomes the content. The go-to-market for knowledge sharing: publish the SPACE framework as a standalone asset, create a 'framework marketplace' concept.
variants.critic: The knowledge management approach has critical gaps that will bite as the project grows. First, there are zero architecture decision records — why was SQLiteStorage added alongside FileSystemStorage? When was it introduced and what triggered the need? Without ADRs, this context is lost. Second, the codebase lacks a CONTRIBUTING.md, so external contributors don't know coding standards, test requirements, or the PR process. Third, there's no changelog — npm version bumps happen but release notes don't exist. The README.md is minimal and doesn't document the architecture, the 326-probe framework structure, or the StorageProvider/LLMProvider extension points. Fourth, knowledge about the framework's probe taxonomy lives only in the JSON files — there's no human-readable explanation of why probes are ordered as they are or what each series accomplishes. The 'documentation as communication' claim is aspirational — the type definitions document the WHAT but not the WHY. The test files document behavior but not design intent. The most significant knowledge gap: there's no documented migration path for framework version upgrades. If the framework schema changes from v2.0.0 to v3.0.0, there's no tooling or documentation to help users migrate their sessions. This is a critical oversight for long-term stewardship.

text: What is the decision-making and escalation process? How are architectural choices made?

choices.text: BDFL — one person makes final decisions with input
Consensus-driven — team agrees, with escalation to lead if deadlocked
ADR-based — proposals, reviews, and recorded Architecture Decision Records

answer:
Decision-making process: BDFL (Benevolent Dictator For Life) — one person makes final decisions.

Architectural decisions are made through: (1) Implement the simplest thing that works. (2) If it needs to change later, the type system makes refactoring safe. (3) The test suite ensures changes don't break existing behavior.

Decision examples:
- "Why no React for the web UI?" → Single HTML file is simpler and sufficient for the current scope.
- "Why no database?" → JSON files are simpler and sufficient for the data volume.
- "Why TypeScript strict mode?" → Catches errors at compile time, worth the stricter coding discipline.
- "Why vitest over jest?" → Better ESM support, faster execution.

Escalation: Not applicable — solo developer. If the project attracts contributors, a lightweight RFC process would be appropriate. Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) would be introduced for significant decisions.

variants.architect: SPACE's architectural decisions follow a 'simplicity first' hierarchy that can be traced through the codebase: (1) Prefer synchronous APIs for CLI tools — FileSystemStorage uses readFileSync/writeFileSync because the CLI is inherently sequential and Node.js async adds complexity without benefit. (2) Prefer composition over inheritance — the Engine composes SessionManager, QuestionRouter, DependencyResolver, and Validator rather than extending them. (3) Prefer explicit contracts over implicit conventions — every interface (StorageProvider, LLMProvider, ExportResult) is explicitly defined in TypeScript. (4) Prefer data-driven configuration over code changes — the framework is JSON, not TypeScript, so non-developers can modify probe content. The decision to use a factory pattern for LLM providers (src/llm/factory.ts) over a plugin registry reflects the principle of controlled extensibility — providers are added by modifying the factory, not by dropping files in a directory. This trades flexibility for predictability. The event system decision (src/engine/core.ts on/emit) enables loose coupling between the engine and intelligence layer but creates an implicit contract on event names — a typed event map would be more robust. Each architectural decision has a corresponding type constraint that enforces it at compile time.
variants.practitioner: Decision-making for a practitioner manifests in concrete choices visible in the code: (1) 'Why Commander over yargs for CLI?' — Commander is used in src/cli/index.ts; the decision is implicit but evident from package.json dependencies. (2) 'Why vitest over jest?' — vitest is configured via package.json scripts; the decision favors ESM compatibility and TypeScript native support. (3) 'Why chalk for terminal colors?' — Used in src/cli/commands/*.ts for colored output. (4) 'Why sql.js over better-sqlite3?' — sql.js in src/storage/sqlite.ts is a pure JavaScript SQLite implementation that doesn't require native compilation, enabling npm install without build tools. (5) 'Why inquirer for prompts?' — Used in src/cli/commands/run.ts for interactive question flow. These decisions weren't documented but are recoverable from package.json and import statements. For a practitioner making a new decision, the pattern is: check if an existing pattern in the codebase covers it (grep for similar code), implement following the same style, and let TypeScript strict mode catch inconsistencies. No formal RFC or proposal process — decisions are made in code.
variants.strategist: Decision-making process should evolve with the project's growth stage. Current: BDFL (Benevolent Dictator For Life) — the sole developer makes all decisions. This is optimal for speed and consistency. When to evolve: (1) At 3+ contributors, introduce an RFC process for architectural changes — a lightweight template (Problem, Proposed Solution, Alternatives, Consequences) stored in docs/rfcs/. (2) At 5+ contributors, establish a core team with merge authority. (3) At 10+ contributors, consider a governance model (e.g., TC39-style stage process for major features). The current decision-making quality is high because the developer is the primary user — decisions are informed by personal experience with the tool. The risk is confirmation bias: decisions that work for the developer may not work for the broader user base. Mitigation: track user issues and feature requests in GitHub, weight decisions by user impact. Key decision framework for the product: prioritize decisions that affect the public API (StorageProvider, LLMProvider, SessionState) over internal implementation details. Public API decisions should have a 6-month stability window. Internal decisions can change freely. The most impactful upcoming decision: whether to support collaborative editing (multi-user sessions) — this fundamentally changes the architecture from single-writer to multi-writer and affects every module.
variants.critic: The BDFL model has produced several decisions that lack justification and may not survive scrutiny. (1) The 'no React for the web UI' decision — stated as 'single HTML file is simpler' — ignores the fact that a 326-probe elicitation flow needs complex state management that vanilla JS handles poorly. The web UI is likely a maintenance burden that grows with each new feature. (2) The 'no database' decision — 'JSON files are simpler' — is contradicted by the fact that SQLiteStorage exists in src/storage/sqlite.ts, meaning a database WAS added. The decision was reversed without documented rationale. (3) The 'no ESLint' decision — justified as 'type checking serves this purpose' — is wrong: TypeScript catches type errors, not style violations, unused imports, or inconsistent naming. (4) The decision to use execSync in GitIntegration (src/integration/git.ts) blocks the event loop and fails silently on timeout — this was chosen for simplicity but creates reliability issues. (5) The event system in core.ts uses string-based event names with no type safety — 'session:created', 'answer:submitted' are magic strings that can be misspelled without detection. The broader critique: most decisions are made for developer convenience rather than user benefit. The architecture should optimize for the user's experience (reliable CLI, fast exports, accurate specs) rather than the developer's comfort (synchronous APIs, minimal abstractions, no linting).

text: How should the system be deployed, released, and updated in production?

choices.text: Manual deploy — push artifacts, restart services, update on schedule
Automated CI/CD — merged to main triggers build + deploy pipeline
Progressive delivery — feature flags, canary releases, gradual rollout

answer:
Deployment and release strategy:

CLI distribution: npm publish to the public registry. Package name: space-cli. Users install globally: "npm install -g space-cli". Updates via "npm update -g space-cli".

Web UI distribution: Git clone. Users clone the repo, run "npm install", then "node web/server.mjs". No separate distribution channel.

Release process:
1. Run full test suite ("npm test")
2. Verify build ("npm run build")
3. Update version in package.json
4. Commit with version tag
5. Run "npm publish"

The prepublishOnly hook runs build + test automatically before publish. If any test fails, publish is blocked.

Rollback: Users can install a specific version: "npm install -g space-cli@2.0.0". Git users can checkout a specific tag.

No canary releases, no staged rollouts, no feature flags for the CLI. The web UI supports feature flags through the SpaceConfig object but this is not exposed to end users.

variants.architect: SPACE's deployment architecture follows the dual-distribution pattern: CLI as npm package, web UI as git clone. The npm distribution pipeline is: source (src/) → TypeScript compilation (tsc) → dist/ directory → npm publish via prepublishOnly script. The bin field in package.json maps 'space' to dist/cli/index.js, enabling global installation. The export strategy uses src/export/index.ts as a facade — exportSession() dispatches to format-specific exporters (JSON, Markdown, YAML, Prompt, HTML, Diff) via a switch statement. Each exporter implements the same ExportResult contract (content, filename, mime_type). The export pipeline could be enhanced with streaming for large outputs — currently exportSession() loads the entire output into a string, which is fine for specs but won't scale for massive projects. The web server in web/server.mjs is a standalone Express-like server that serves the SPA and REST API — it has no dependency on the CLI's build pipeline. This means the web UI and CLI can be deployed independently, which is architecturally sound but creates version divergence risk. The release strategy should include a version handshake: the web server checks that the framework version it serves matches the CLI's framework version.
variants.practitioner: Deployment steps for the CLI: (1) Ensure tests pass: 'npm test'. (2) Ensure build succeeds: 'npm run build' (runs tsc). (3) Verify types: 'npx tsc --noEmit'. (4) Update version in package.json (currently 2.1.0). (5) Commit and tag: 'git tag v2.1.0'. (6) Publish: 'npm publish' (prepublishOnly runs build+test automatically). The package.json 'files' field includes only 'dist/', 'LICENSE', 'README.md' — ensuring only compiled code ships. The 'main' field points to dist/index.js (the public API) and 'types' to dist/index.d.ts. For the web UI: copy web/ directory to target machine, run 'node web/server.mjs', access at http://localhost:3000. The web server reads from ~/.space/projects/ by default. For updates: users run 'npm update -g space-cli'. The CLI includes a VERSION constant in src/cli/index.ts (currently '2.1.0') — this should be derived from package.json at build time to prevent version drift. Testing deployment: 'npm pack' creates a .tgz file that can be installed locally via 'npm install ./space-cli-2.1.0.tgz' for smoke testing.
variants.strategist: The deployment strategy directly impacts user acquisition and retention. Current: npm global install is frictionless for developers — 'npm install -g space-cli' is a one-command onboarding experience. This is the optimal distribution channel for developer tools. Release cadence recommendation: (1) Patch releases (bug fixes): weekly, automated via CI/CD. (2) Minor releases (new features): bi-weekly, requires manual review. (3) Major releases (breaking changes): quarterly, with migration guide. Success metrics for deployment: (1) Time from commit to npm availability (target: <5 minutes with CI/CD), (2) Install success rate (target: >99%), (3) Update adoption rate (target: >70% within 1 week of release). The web UI deployment is a growth opportunity — currently it requires git clone + npm install, which is 3+ commands. A hosted version (Vercel/Railway) would eliminate this friction and enable a freemium model. The deployment infrastructure should support: (1) CLI: npm (current), Homebrew (future), standalone binary (future via pkg/nexe), (2) Web: self-hosted (current), hosted SaaS (future), Docker container (future). Each additional distribution channel increases user acquisition by ~30% based on developer tool market benchmarks.
variants.critic: The deployment strategy has several fragilities. (1) The prepublishOnly script runs build+test, but doesn't verify the binary works — 'npm pack' followed by 'npm install -g ./space-cli-*.tgz' should be part of the release checklist. (2) The VERSION constant in src/cli/index.ts is hardcoded as '2.1.0' — if the developer forgets to update it, the CLI reports the wrong version. This should be injected at build time from package.json. (3) There's no CI/CD pipeline — publishing requires manual npm publish, which means: (a) a developer must have npm credentials, (b) there's no automated testing on the publish artifact, (c) there's no rollback mechanism. (4) The web UI deployment (git clone + node web/server.mjs) has no process management — if the server crashes, it stays down until manually restarted. PM2 or systemd should be recommended. (5) The dual distribution model (CLI via npm, web via git) means users might run different versions of the CLI and web UI, leading to schema incompatibilities. (6) npm doesn't support atomic deployments — a failed publish can leave the registry in an inconsistent state.
